svg.title: The cost of each additional nine of availability, and where redundancy stops paying
svg.desc: Four rows pair an availability target with the downtime it permits per year and what that target typically buys, from redundant power supplies at 99% up to process, drills and supply chain at 99.999%. A small bar chart shows two links as standard, four needing justification, and five or more adding more complexity than benefit.
svg.text: Each additional nine costs more than the previous one
Eliminating a double failure costs exponentially more than eliminating a single failure — decide which one the business actually needs
What the target buys
3.65 days of downtime a year
redundant power supplies, a spare switch on the shelf
8.76 hours a year
device redundancy, FHRP, failover that has been tested
52.6 minutes a year
path redundancy, tuned convergence, monitoring you trust
5.3 minutes a year
process, drills, change control, supply chain, spare inventory
How much redundancy is too much?
2 parallel links — the standard
adequate
4 parallel links — needs justification
justify it
5 or more — complexity in search of a problem
no
Too much is not a count of links. It is where
added complexity and cost stop paying — and
nobody left can predict the failure behaviour.
Note the asymmetry: going from 99.99% to 99.999% is not "one more redundant device". It is change windows, rehearsed failovers,
contractual spare parts and a team that practices. Nine tenths of the cost of the last nine is organisational, not capital.
Ask the business to name the outage it is willing to survive, in hours — not to name a percentage. Then design to the sentence, not the number.
